items.meta_title: Give VpnHood! SERVER a Domain Name and a Trusted Certificate | VpnHood!
items.meta_description: Give VpnHood! SERVER a domain name with a certificate from a certificate authority, on a managed server or a standalone one, so a connection to it looks like a visit to an ordinary website.
items.title: Use a domain name and a trusted certificate
items.lead: Out of the box, the server presents a self-signed certificate with a made-up name. Give it a domain name you own, with a certificate from a certificate authority, and a connection to it looks like a visit to an ordinary website.
items.why_keys: Apps check the certificate the way a browser does, by the authority that signed it and the name it carries, so keys made after the change keep working when the certificate is renewed.
items.why_ips: A domain does not hide the server, though: it points at the server's IP address, and the keys still carry that address. To keep your users connected when the address is blocked, put the server behind a reverse proxy, which needs this certificate first.
items.req_domain: A domain or a subdomain you control, such as [domain_example]. Use a single name, not a wildcard, and one that does not say VPN: apps send it in clear at the start of every connection, where the network can read it.
items.req_dns: A DNS record that points it straight at the server's connection IP: an A record, and an AAAA record if the server has an IPv6 address. To put Cloudflare in front of the server, finish this page first, then turn its proxy on.
items.mgr_box_title: Easily use your own domain with VpnHood! MANAGER
items.mgr_box_desc: Instead of the steps below, let the free web panel get a trusted certificate for your domain from Let's Encrypt, and renew it by itself before it expires.
items.file_cert: A standalone server cannot get a certificate by itself. Get one for the domain from a certificate authority, as a PFX file with its private key, and put it in place of [server_cert_pfx], under the same name.
items.file_settings: Then put the file's password in [setting_ssl_password] and set [setting_is_valid_host_name] to [json_true], both under [setting_file_access_manager] in [server_appsettings]. A new install has no such file: create it, and from then on the server uses it in place of the settings it was installed with.
items.caption_file: The whole file, with your certificate's password in place of the example
items.file_name: The server takes the domain from the certificate itself, so there is no setting for it.
items.file_restart: Restart the server with [server_restart_linux], or with [docker_restart] in Docker. With a wrong password it does not start, and its log says [log_could_not_start]
items.file_keys: Keys made before the change stop working, as they expect the old certificate. Print each of them again and give your users the new key: its options and its usage stay the same. A key's ID is the name of its file in [server_access_dir], without [key_file_ext].
items.caption_print: List the keys, then print one again by its ID
items.file_docker: In Docker, run the same through [docker_exec_supervisor], as for [vhserver_gen].
items.file_renew: The new keys carry the domain and no longer depend on the certificate itself, so they keep working when you renew it: put the new file in place and restart the server.
